61116.e: Because of subsidence caused by mining, no underground sewers could be built, so sewage flowed openly in the Emscher. In the Emscher conversion, the sewage was moved into an underground channel and the river was restored to a natural state.
61116.m: The Emscher turned from a sewer back into a river.

61117.q: What is the association of the towns and districts of the Ruhr called, which among other things is responsible for regional planning?
61117.e: The Ruhr Regional Association, based in Essen, is responsible for regional planning for the Ruhr metropolis. It also promotes the economy, tourism and open spaces in the region.
61117.m: The Ruhr Regional Association plans the Ruhr metropolis jointly.

61118.q: What is the tourist network called that links former industrial sites in the Ruhr such as collieries, ironworks and gasometers?
61118.e: The Industrial Heritage Trail (Route der Industriekultur) links anchor points such as the Gasometer Oberhausen and the Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord. It shows how industrial monuments are reused for tourism and culture.
61118.m: The Industrial Heritage Trail turns old industrial sites into places to visit.

61119.q: Which landscape park was created on the site of a closed ironworks in Duisburg-Meiderich?
61119.e: The Meiderich ironworks closed in 1985 and was turned into a park. Today its blast furnaces serve as viewpoints, climbing walls and event venues.
61119.m: In the Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord, a blast furnace has become a leisure facility.

61120.q: Which of the following is one of the four fundamental freedoms of the EU single market?
61120.e: The four fundamental freedoms are the free movement of goods, persons, services and capital. They are meant to make the single market work like a single national market.
61120.m: Goods, persons, services and capital move freely in the single market.

61121.q: Since when has the European single market officially been regarded as complete?
61121.e: The Single European Act set the goal of completing the single market by the end of 1992. On 1 January 1993 most border controls on goods ended.
61121.m: The single market started on 1 January 1993.

61122.q: Which treaty of 1986 set the goal of completing the single market by the end of 1992?
61122.e: The Single European Act came into force in 1987. It made majority decisions in the Council easier, so that the many single market laws could be passed more quickly.
61122.m: The Single European Act paved the way for the single market.

61123.q: Which principle did the Cassis de Dijon ruling of the European Court of Justice in 1979 establish?
61123.e: A product lawfully sold in one member state may in principle also be sold in the others. The case was about a French liqueur that had too little alcohol for the rules in Germany.
61123.m: What is allowed in one EU country may in principle be sold everywhere.

61124.q: What does it mean that Switzerland has applied the Cassis de Dijon principle unilaterally since 2010?
a: Many EU products may be sold in Switzerland without extra testing
Swiss products may enter the EU without testing
Switzerland adopts all EU laws automatically
Switzerland has given up all customs duties
61124.e: Since July 2010 many products lawfully sold in the EU may also be sold in Switzerland. Unilaterally means that the EU does not automatically grant Switzerland the same.
61124.m: In 2010 Switzerland adopted the Cassis de Dijon principle unilaterally.

61125.q: Which three countries take part in the single market through the European Economic Area without being EU members?
61125.e: The EEA has existed since 1994 and extends the single market to these three EFTA states. Switzerland rejected joining the EEA in the referendum of 6 December 1992.
61125.m: Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are in the single market through the EEA.

61126.q: Through which set of agreements did Switzerland gain, among other things, free movement of persons with the EU in 2002?
61126.e: The Bilaterals I were signed in 1999 and came into force in 2002. They include seven agreements, among them free movement of persons, land transport and technical barriers to trade.
61126.m: The Bilaterals I opened parts of the single market to Switzerland.

61127.q: What distinguishes a customs union like the EU from a simple free trade area?
61127.e: In a free trade area, each country sets its own customs duties for non-member countries. In a customs union, a single tariff applies to non-member countries.
61127.m: A customs union has a common external tariff.

61128.q: What are barriers to trade such as different technical standards or approval procedures called?
61128.e: Non-tariff barriers are not customs duties, but they also hinder trade. The single market reduced them through harmonisation and mutual recognition.
61128.m: Different standards can slow down trade just like customs duties.

61129.q: Since when have euro notes and coins been in circulation?
61129.e: The euro was introduced as book money on 1 January 1999. Coins and banknotes followed on 1 January 2002.
61129.m: Euro coins and notes have existed since 2002.

61130.q: Which country introduced the euro on 1 January 2026 as the 21st member?
61130.e: Bulgaria gave up the lev, which had previously been pegged to the euro. This gives the eurozone 21 members (as of 2026).
61130.m: Bulgaria has been a member of the eurozone since 2026.

61131.q: Who forms the ECB Governing Council together with the six-member Executive Board?
a: The governors of the national central banks
The finance ministers of the euro countries
The members of the EU Commission
The heads of government of the euro countries
61131.e: The Governing Council is made up of the members of the Executive Board and the governors of the central banks of all euro countries. It decides on key interest rates and is politically independent.
61131.m: The ECB Governing Council consists of the Executive Board and the national central bank governors.

61132.q: Under the Maastricht criteria, what is the maximum annual budget deficit of a euro country?
61132.e: The deficit limit is 3 per cent of gross domestic product. The 60 per cent limit applies to total debt.
61132.m: The deficit should stay below 3 per cent of GDP.

61133.q: What is the European Central Bank explicitly forbidden to do under the EU treaty?
61133.e: The ban on monetary financing of governments is meant to stop governments from funding themselves by printing money. The ECB may only buy government bonds on the secondary market.
61133.m: The ECB may not finance governments directly.

61134.q: At what exchange rate did the Swiss National Bank defend a minimum rate against the euro from 2011 to 2015?
61134.e: In September 2011 the SNB introduced the minimum rate to slow down the heavily overvalued franc. On 15 January 2015 it surprisingly removed it.
61134.m: From 2011 to 2015 the SNB kept the euro at at least 1.20 francs.

61135.q: Which institution was created in 2012 as a permanent rescue fund for euro countries in difficulty?
61135.e: The ESM lends money to euro countries with financing problems, on condition that they carry out reforms. It was set up as a result of the sovereign debt crisis that began in Greece in 2010.
61135.m: The ESM is the eurozone's permanent rescue fund.

61136.q: What inflation target does the European Central Bank aim for in the medium term?
61136.e: Since its strategy review in 2021, the ECB has aimed for a symmetrical inflation rate of 2 per cent. Price stability is its main goal.
61136.m: The ECB aims for inflation of 2 per cent.

61137.q: Which tool does a country lose when it adopts the euro?
a: Its own monetary and interest rate policy
The right to its own taxes
61137.e: In the euro area, the ECB Governing Council sets interest rates and the money supply for all members together. A single country can also no longer devalue its currency to become more competitive.
61137.m: With the euro, a country gives up its own monetary policy.

61138.q: Which condition must a country meet, among others, before introducing the euro?
a: Its currency must be stable against the euro for two years
It must have at least 10 million inhabitants
It must be completely free of debt
It must be a member of NATO
61138.e: The currency takes part in Exchange Rate Mechanism II for at least two years and may only move a little around a central rate against the euro. Other criteria concern inflation, interest rates, the deficit and debt.
61138.m: Before the euro, a currency must stay stable against the euro for two years.

61139.q: Who owns the majority of the Port of Rotterdam Authority (Havenbedrijf Rotterdam)?
61139.e: The Port Authority is a public limited company owned about 70 per cent by the municipality of Rotterdam and about 30 per cent by the Dutch state. It manages the port area and leases land to companies.
61139.m: The Port of Rotterdam Authority belongs mainly to the city.

61140.q: Why did Rotterdam build new port land out into the North Sea with Maasvlakte 2?
a: For terminals for ever larger container ships
For a nature reserve without shipping
For new residential areas by the beach
61140.e: Container ships keep getting bigger and need deep water and lots of space. That is why land was built up in the sea. Maasvlakte 2 opened in 2013.
61140.m: Rotterdam built new port land in the sea for giant ships.

61141.q: Which canal connects Rotterdam directly with the North Sea?
61141.e: The Nieuwe Waterweg was built in the 19th century to improve access to the North Sea. It links the Rhine-Meuse estuary with the open sea.
61141.m: The Nieuwe Waterweg is Rotterdam's access to the sea.

61142.q: Why is the port of Rotterdam also important for Switzerland's supplies?
a: It is connected to Basel via the Rhine
It is partly owned by the Swiss Confederation
It is connected to the Aare
61142.e: Inland vessels carry goods such as containers and mineral oil along the Rhine to the Swiss Rhine ports in Basel. The Rhine is therefore Switzerland's access to the sea.
61142.m: Switzerland is connected to the port of Rotterdam via the Rhine.

61143.q: How is Rotterdam protected from storm floods at its entrance from the North Sea?
a: With a huge movable storm surge barrier
With a fixed dam that permanently blocks the entrance
With floating houses throughout the port
Not at all, the city lies high above the sea
61143.e: The Maeslantkering in the Nieuwe Waterweg consists of two huge gates that are only closed during a storm flood. Otherwise the entrance stays open for ships. It is part of the Delta Works.
61143.m: A movable storm surge barrier protects Rotterdam during storm floods.

61144.q: What does the unit TEU, used to measure container handling, mean?
61144.e: TEU stands for twenty-foot equivalent unit. A 40-foot container counts as two TEU.

61145.q: Which industry has settled particularly strongly in the port area of Rotterdam?
61145.e: The port has several large refineries and chemical plants that process imported crude oil. Pipelines run from there to Germany and Belgium, among other places.
61145.m: Rotterdam is a centre of oil processing.

61146.q: Why was a freight-only railway line built from the port of Rotterdam to Germany?
a: To shift goods from road to rail
To get passengers to Paris faster
To deliver coal to Great Britain
61146.e: The Betuweroute opened in 2007 and is for freight trains only. It connects the port with the hinterland in Germany and so takes pressure off the roads.
61146.m: A dedicated freight railway carries port goods from Rotterdam to Germany.

61147.q: Which port area was built at the river mouth from the 1950s to take large tankers, and has a name meaning “Gateway to Europe”?
61147.e: Europoort was built closer to the sea because ships kept getting bigger. Over time the port thus moved from the city towards the North Sea.
61147.m: Europoort is Rotterdam's gateway to Europe.

61148.q: In which year was Airbus Industrie founded as a European joint venture?
61148.e: Airbus Industrie was founded in 1970 by French and German companies, and Spain and Great Britain joined later. The aim was a European counterweight to the US manufacturers.
61148.m: Airbus was founded in 1970 as a European project.

61149.q: What was the first Airbus aircraft?
61149.e: The A300 first flew in 1972 and was the world's first twin-engined wide-body aircraft. It laid the foundation for the later Airbus models.
61149.m: The A300 was the first Airbus aircraft.

61150.q: Which wide-body aircraft was assembled in Toulouse and discontinued in 2021 after fewer than 300 had been built?
61150.e: The A380 is the largest passenger aircraft in the world. Because of low demand, production ended in 2021.
61150.m: The A380 was built in Toulouse and discontinued in 2021.

61151.q: Apart from Toulouse, which German site is a main site for final assembly of the A320 family?
61151.e: At Hamburg-Finkenwerder, aircraft of the A320 family are assembled and delivered. Other German plants such as Bremen or Stade make components.
61151.m: Hamburg is the most important German Airbus site.

61152.q: What is the special aircraft called that Airbus uses to carry large aircraft parts between its plants?
61152.e: The Beluga has a huge, bulging fuselage that looks like a white whale. It carries parts such as wings and fuselage sections from different countries to Toulouse or Hamburg.
61152.m: The Beluga carries aircraft parts between Airbus plants.

61153.q: Which company is Airbus's main competitor for large airliners?
61153.e: Airbus and Boeing share most of the market for large passenger aircraft. This is therefore called a duopoly.
61153.m: Airbus and Boeing form a duopoly.

61154.q: Why are the large Airbus assembly halls in Toulouse right next to Toulouse-Blagnac airport?
a: Finished aircraft can take off directly for their first flight
The airport supplies electricity to the halls
Only there is the ground flat enough for halls
61154.e: The final assembly lines are right next to the runway. This means new aircraft can be tested and delivered to customers without being transported.
61154.m: Airbus assembles its aircraft at Toulouse-Blagnac.

61155.q: Which famous supersonic aircraft was also assembled in Toulouse in France?
61155.e: Concorde was built jointly by France and Great Britain. The French aircraft were made in Toulouse, the British ones near Bristol.
61155.m: The French Concordes were built in Toulouse.

61156.q: What is the French region around Toulouse called, where aerospace is an important industry?
61156.e: Toulouse is the capital of the Occitania region. Together with Bordeaux, it forms a large aerospace cluster with many suppliers.
61156.m: Occitania, with Toulouse, is a centre of the aviation industry.

61157.q: In which city does Volkswagen AG have its headquarters?
61157.e: Wolfsburg was founded in 1938 specially for the Volkswagen factory. The main plant is one of the largest car factories in the world.

61158.q: Which inventor applied for a patent in 1886 for a vehicle with a gas engine that is considered the first modern car?
61158.e: The Benz Patent-Motorwagen Number 1 is considered the birth certificate of the car. Carl Benz built it in Mannheim.
61158.m: Carl Benz received the patent for the first car in 1886.

61159.q: Which city is the home of Mercedes-Benz and Porsche?
61159.e: Stuttgart and the region along the Neckar are a centre of the car and supplier industry. The supplier Bosch is also based nearby.
61159.m: Stuttgart is a German car city with Mercedes-Benz and Porsche.

61160.q: Which German company is the largest car parts supplier in the world?
61160.e: Bosch supplies fuel injection systems, brake technology and electronics, among other things, to many car makers. Its headquarters is in Gerlingen near Stuttgart.
61160.m: Bosch is the world's largest car parts supplier.

61161.q: Which scandal shook the German car industry in 2015?
a: Manipulated emissions figures for diesel cars
Faked crash tests for small cars
61161.e: Volkswagen had used software that recognised emissions tests and then released less nitrogen oxide. The diesel scandal cost the company billions.
61161.m: The 2015 diesel scandal involved manipulated emissions figures.

61162.q: Where did Tesla open its first European car factory in 2022?
61162.e: The Gigafactory in Grünheide in Brandenburg makes electric cars. Its construction was controversial because of water use and the clearing of forest.
61162.m: Since 2022 Tesla has built electric cars in Grünheide near Berlin.

61163.q: In which Bavarian city does Audi have its headquarters?
61163.e: Audi is part of the Volkswagen Group and has its main plant in Ingolstadt on the Danube. BMW, by contrast, is based in Munich.
61163.m: Audi has its headquarters in Ingolstadt.

61164.q: What is the production principle called in which suppliers deliver parts to the assembly line exactly when they are needed?
61164.e: With just-in-time, warehouses are saved because parts are delivered exactly on time. But this makes production vulnerable to supply disruptions, for example when there is a shortage of chips.
61164.m: Just-in-time means delivery at exactly the right moment.

61165.q: Which technological change has been the biggest challenge for the German car industry since the 2010s?
a: The switch to wood gas generators
61165.e: Electric cars need no combustion engines or gearboxes, which German manufacturers and suppliers are strong in. At the same time, competition from China and the USA is growing.
61165.m: Electric mobility is fundamentally changing the German car industry.

61166.q: What was the main aim of the Common Agricultural Policy when it was introduced in 1962?
a: To secure food supplies and stabilise farmers' incomes
To get food from overseas as far as possible
61166.e: After the Second World War, food supplies in Europe were still uncertain. The CAP was meant to secure enough food at affordable prices and give farmers a stable income.
61166.m: The Common Agricultural Policy was meant to secure food and farmers' incomes.

61167.q: What does the so-called second pillar of the Common Agricultural Policy support?
61167.e: The first pillar mainly covers direct payments and market measures. The second pillar supports rural development, for example environmental schemes, investments and village development.
61167.m: The second pillar of the CAP strengthens rural areas.

61168.q: What caused the so-called butter mountains and milk lakes in the 1970s and 1980s?
61168.e: Because the EC guaranteed to buy from farmers at fixed intervention prices, more was produced than was needed. The surpluses had to be stored at great cost or exported cheaply.
61168.m: Guaranteed prices led to butter mountains and milk lakes.

61169.q: What was the purpose of the milk quota that applied in the EU from 1984 to 2015?
a: It limited the amount of milk each farm could produce
It set the fat content of milk
It banned milk imports from Switzerland
It guaranteed free milk to all schoolchildren
61169.e: Because of guaranteed prices, too much milk was being produced. The quota set a maximum amount for each farm to prevent surpluses such as the milk lakes. It was abolished in 2015.
61169.m: The milk quota was meant to prevent milk surpluses.

61170.q: What changed fundamentally with the EU's big agricultural reform of 1992?
a: Direct payments replaced high guaranteed prices
Farmers no longer received any money at all
The EU bought up all farms
61170.e: Guaranteed prices were lowered so that fewer surpluses would arise. In compensation, farmers received direct payments. The reform is named after EU Agriculture Commissioner Ray MacSharry.
61170.m: From 1992 direct payments gradually replaced the high guaranteed prices.

61171.q: What does the decoupling of direct payments, introduced with the 2003 reform, mean?
a: Payments no longer depend on the amount produced
Payments only go to organic farms
Payments are only made for exports
61171.e: Since decoupling, farms receive money mainly per area, regardless of how much they produce. This is meant to make production more market-oriented.
61171.m: Decoupled payments no longer reward quantity.

61172.q: What happens in the EU if a farm breaks environmental or animal welfare rules?
a: It receives extra money for improvements
It immediately loses its land to the state
Nothing, the payments do not depend on it
61172.e: Direct payments are linked to compliance with rules on the environment, animal welfare and consumer protection. This principle was called cross-compliance; since 2023 it has been called conditionality.
61172.m: EU farm money is only paid if environmental and animal welfare rules are followed.

61173.q: Roughly what share of the EU budget goes on agricultural policy today?
61173.e: In the 1980s more than half the budget still went to agriculture. Today it is about a third, while the share of cohesion policy has grown.
61173.m: About a third of the EU budget goes to agriculture.

61174.q: Why were the EU's export subsidies for agricultural products strongly criticised?
a: They harmed farmers in developing countries
They made food in Africa much more expensive
They only financed large farms in the USA
61174.e: Subsidised surpluses were exported at prices below the cost of production. Farmers in poorer countries could not compete with these low prices.
61174.m: Subsidised exports weakened farmers in poor countries.

61175.q: Which stretch of the Playa de Palma is known in German-speaking countries as the very symbol of party tourism?
61175.e: The name comes from the beach kiosk Balneario 6 near S'Arenal. For years the municipality of Palma has been trying to curb heavy drinking with stricter rules.
61175.m: Ballermann stands for party tourism on Mallorca.

61176.q: Why is Palma airport much busier in summer than in winter?
a: Because of beach tourism in the summer season
Because of flight bans in winter
61176.e: Millions of tourists arrive every year through Son Sant Joan airport, most of them between May and October. In winter it is much quieter.
61176.m: Mallorca's airport depends on summer tourism.

61177.q: What is the uncontrolled building-up of coasts with hotels and holiday resorts called, named after the Balearic Islands?
61177.e: The term arose because whole stretches of coast on Mallorca were built up from the 1960s. Today it is also used for other tourist regions.
61177.m: Balearisation means the building-up of entire coastlines.

61178.q: Which development triggered mass tourism on Mallorca from the 1950s and 1960s?
a: Building a bridge to the mainland
61178.e: Cheap charter flights made holidays in the south affordable for large parts of the population. Tour operators offered flight and hotel as a package.
61178.m: Charter flights and package holidays brought mass tourism to Mallorca.

61179.q: What did the Balearic Islands introduce in 2016 to raise money for environmental and tourism projects?
a: A tourist tax per overnight stay
An entry fee at the port
61179.e: The so-called ecotasa is charged per person per night, depending on the type of accommodation. The money is meant to go into sustainable tourism and environmental protection.
61179.m: Since 2016 Mallorca has charged a tourist tax.

61180.q: How, among other things, is the high demand for water during the tourist season met on Mallorca?
a: With glacier water from the Alps
61180.e: Hotels, pools and golf courses use a lot of water, while the island gets little rain. Besides groundwater, desalination plants supply drinking water.
61180.m: Desalination plants help against water shortages on Mallorca.

61181.q: Which economic problem is caused by the strongly seasonal tourism on Mallorca?
61181.e: Many hotels and restaurants close outside the summer season. Workers often have no job then, which is why there are efforts to spread tourism across the year.
61181.m: Seasonal tourism leads to unemployment in winter.

61182.q: What were large demonstrations by local people on Mallorca in 2024 directed against?
61182.e: Tens of thousands protested in Palma against overcrowded places and rising housing costs. Holiday flats for tourists reduce the housing available to local people.
61182.m: On Mallorca, local people are protesting against overtourism.

61183.q: What do you call an economy like Mallorca's that depends very heavily on a single industry?
61183.e: A large part of economic output and jobs depends on tourism. Crises such as the coronavirus pandemic hit such a monostructure especially hard.
61183.m: A monostructure makes a region vulnerable to crises.

61184.q: Which nickname is often used for the City of London because of its area?
61184.e: The City covers only about 2.9 square kilometres, roughly one square mile. Even so, it is one of the most important financial centres in the world.
61184.m: Because of its area, the City of London is called the Square Mile.

61185.q: Which central bank has its seat in Threadneedle Street in the City of London?
61185.e: The Bank of England was founded in 1694. Its nickname is “the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street”.
61185.m: The Bank of England is in the City of London.

61186.q: What is the deregulation of the London financial market in 1986 under Margaret Thatcher called?
61186.e: On 27 October 1986 fixed commissions were abolished and electronic share trading was introduced. Afterwards many foreign banks moved to London.
61186.m: The Big Bang of 1986 opened up the London financial market.

61187.q: Which business district in the former Docklands developed into London's second financial centre?
61187.e: Canary Wharf was built from the late 1980s on the site of disused docks. Many major banks have their tower blocks there.
61187.m: Canary Wharf is London's second financial centre.

61188.q: Which right, which had allowed them to do business throughout the EU, did financial firms in London lose because of Brexit?
61188.e: With the EU passport, a bank licensed in London could operate in all EU countries. After Brexit, some firms moved parts of their business to Dublin, Frankfurt, Paris or Amsterdam.
61188.m: With Brexit, the City lost EU passporting.

61189.q: Which famous insurance market is based in the City of London?
61189.e: Lloyd's began in the 17th century in a coffee house where ship insurance was traded. Today it is a marketplace for specialist insurance.
61189.m: Lloyd's of London is a famous insurance market.

61190.q: Which office is at the head of the City of London Corporation?
61190.e: The Lord Mayor is elected every year and represents the financial centre at home and abroad. The Mayor of London, by contrast, is mayor of the whole of Greater London.
61190.m: The City has its own head, the Lord Mayor.

61191.q: Roughly how many people live in the City of London?
61191.e: The City has only a few thousand residents, but hundreds of thousands of commuters work there. It is full during the day and rather empty at night and at weekends.
61191.m: Far more people work in the City than live there.

61192.q: In which area of the financial market is London the largest trading centre in the world?
61192.e: According to surveys by the Bank for International Settlements, more currency is traded in London than anywhere else. The reasons are its time zone between Asia and America and its concentration of banks.
61192.m: London is the world's largest foreign exchange trading centre.

61193.q: Which regions are typically counted as part of the so-called Third Italy?
61193.e: The Third Italy covers regions in the north-east and centre of the country. They lie between the old industrial triangle and the south.
61193.m: Emilia-Romagna, Tuscany and Veneto form the Third Italy.

61194.q: Which area is distinguished from the Third Italy as the First Italy?
a: The industrial triangle of Milan, Turin and Genoa
The islands of Sicily and Sardinia
The Alpine region of South Tyrol
61194.e: The First Italy is the classic industrial north-west with large firms such as Fiat. The Second Italy is the economically weaker south.
61194.m: The First Italy is the industrial triangle in the north-west.

61195.q: Which type of business especially shapes the economy in the Third Italy?
61195.e: Many specialised small and medium-sized businesses, often family-owned, are typical. They work together in networks and are flexible.
61195.m: Small family businesses shape the economy of the Third Italy.

61196.q: What are the local concentrations of specialised businesses in the same industry in the Third Italy called?
61196.e: In an industrial district, many firms in one industry work closely together and compete at the same time. Knowledge, skilled workers and suppliers are all available locally.
61196.m: Industrial districts bring many businesses of one industry together in one place.

61197.q: Why do people in Italy speak of a “Third Italy”?
a: It differs from the industrial north-west and the south
It was Italy's third capital region
It was the third area to join Italy
It is Italy's third largest region
61197.e: The sociologist Arnaldo Bagnasco coined the term in 1977. Alongside the industrial triangle in the north-west and the Mezzogiorno, he saw a third, separate economic model.
61197.m: The Third Italy has its own economic model between the industrial north and the south.

61198.q: For which industry is the Tuscan town of Prato known as an industrial district?
61198.e: Prato has been a centre of wool processing for centuries. Today many Chinese businesses also work there in clothing manufacture.
61198.m: Prato is a centre of the textile industry.

61199.q: Why do machine builders also settle in an industrial district such as the tile centre of Sassuolo?
a: Because they find many customers and skilled workers there
Because the state tells them where to locate
Because machines may only be built there
61199.e: Italian tile production is concentrated around Sassuolo. Suppliers and machine builders benefit from being close to their customers and from the know-how in the region.
61199.m: In industrial districts, businesses, suppliers and skilled workers attract each other.

61200.q: Which economic area in Emilia-Romagna is known for sports car makers such as Ferrari and Lamborghini?
61200.e: Ferrari in Maranello, Lamborghini and Ducati are located around Modena and Bologna. The region offers highly specialised suppliers and skilled workers.

61201.q: What is the successful model of businesses in the Third Italy called, which relies on adapting quickly to customers' wishes?
61201.e: Instead of large series, the businesses produce smaller, specialised quantities and change their range quickly. This is seen as the opposite of Fordist mass production.
61201.m: Flexible specialisation is the recipe for success of the Third Italy.

61202.q: Which member states can receive money from the EU Cohesion Fund?
a: Countries below 90 per cent of the EU average GNI
Countries with more than 10 million inhabitants
Only the founding states of the EU
61202.e: What counts is gross national income per head. If it is below 90 per cent of the EU average, a country is eligible for funding.
61202.m: The Cohesion Fund helps countries below 90 per cent of the EU average.

61203.q: What does the Cohesion Fund mainly spend its money on?
61203.e: The Cohesion Fund mainly finances trans-European transport networks and environmental infrastructure. Examples are motorways, railway lines and sewage treatment plants.
61203.m: The Cohesion Fund builds transport routes and environmental infrastructure.

61204.q: Which EU structural fund was set up in 1975 to reduce regional imbalances?
61204.e: The ERDF supports investment in businesses, research and infrastructure in weaker regions. Today it is the largest fund of regional policy.
61204.m: The ERDF has supported weaker regions since 1975.

61205.q: From which value is a region considered less developed in EU regional policy?
a: GDP per head below 75 per cent of the EU average
GDP per head below 50 per cent of the EU average
61205.e: Regions below 75 per cent of average GDP per head receive the highest funding rates. GDP is measured in purchasing power standards.
61205.m: Below 75 per cent of the EU average, a region counts as less developed.

61206.q: What is the EU's NUTS classification used for?
a: To divide regions comparably for statistics and funding
To set customs duties at the external borders
To count the official languages of the regions
To create constituencies for the European Parliament
61206.e: The NUTS classification divides Europe into areas of different sizes. Decisions on which regions receive how much funding are usually made at the NUTS 2 level.
61206.m: NUTS divides Europe into comparable regions.

61207.q: Which EU country received the most money from cohesion policy in the funding periods from 2014?
61207.e: As a large country with many eligible regions, Poland is the largest recipient. The money was used, for example, to modernise motorways and railway lines.
61207.m: Poland is the largest recipient of EU cohesion policy.

61208.q: What do EU countries usually have to contribute themselves for projects funded by regional policy?
a: The entire cost, paid back later
61208.e: The EU usually pays only part of a project, and the rest is borne by the state, region or municipality. EU money is meant to add to their own spending, not replace it.
61208.m: EU funding requires the country to make its own contribution.

61209.q: What is the EU programme for cross-border cooperation called, in which Switzerland also takes part?
61209.e: Interreg supports projects across national borders, for example on the Upper Rhine or around Lake Geneva. Switzerland takes part as part of its New Regional Policy.
61209.m: Interreg links border regions, including with Switzerland.

61210.q: What was Switzerland's first contribution to reducing economic inequalities in the new EU member states from 2004 called?
61210.e: With the enlargement contribution, Switzerland supported projects in the countries that joined the EU in 2004 and later. Voters accepted it in 2006, and it amounted to about 1.3 billion francs.
61210.m: With the enlargement contribution, Switzerland supported new EU member states.

61211.q: Which oil field in the Norwegian sector of the North Sea was discovered in 1969 and began Norway's oil age?
61211.e: Ekofisk was discovered by Phillips Petroleum at the end of 1969 and produced oil from 1971. It was the first large find in Norwegian waters.
61211.m: Norway's oil age began with the discovery of Ekofisk in 1969.

61212.q: Which important crude oil benchmark is named after a British North Sea oil field?
61212.e: Brent is named after the Brent field east of the Shetland Islands, discovered in 1971. It serves worldwide as a price benchmark for crude oil.
61212.m: The Brent oil price is named after a North Sea oil field.

61213.q: Which disaster on a platform in the British North Sea claimed 167 lives in 1988?
61213.e: On 6 July 1988 the Piper Alpha platform exploded and burned out, and 167 people died. It is still the worst disaster in offshore oil production.
61213.m: Piper Alpha is the worst disaster in the offshore oil industry.

61214.q: On which principle was the North Sea floor divided between the neighbouring countries for oil production?
a: Proportional principle by length of coastline
61214.e: Based on the 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf, the sea floor was divided along median lines between the coasts. That is why Norway and Great Britain received large shares.
61214.m: The North Sea floor is divided along median lines between the coastal states.

61215.q: What is the Norwegian, majority state-owned oil company called that was named Statoil until 2018?
61215.e: Statoil was founded in 1972 as a state oil company and renamed Equinor in 2018. The Norwegian state holds the majority of the shares.
61215.m: The former oil company Statoil is now called Equinor.

61216.q: Which term describes the weakening of a country's industry through sudden wealth from raw materials and a strong currency?
61216.e: The term was coined in 1977 in “The Economist”, looking at the Netherlands after the natural gas discoveries near Groningen. High raw material exports pushed up the currency and harmed other export industries.
61216.m: Dutch disease describes the damage done by one-sided wealth from raw materials.

61217.q: Over which disused oil installation was there a big conflict between Shell and Greenpeace in 1995?
61217.e: Shell wanted to sink the Brent Spar oil storage buoy in the Atlantic. After protests and boycotts it was dismantled on land, and in 1998 the OSPAR states banned the sinking of such installations.
61217.m: The dispute over Brent Spar led to a ban on sinking oil platforms at sea.

61218.q: How has British oil production in the North Sea developed since about 2000?
a: It has stayed exactly the same
61218.e: British production reached its peak around 1999 and has fallen considerably since then. Since the mid-2000s Great Britain has once again had to import more oil than it produces.
61218.m: The British North Sea is past its production peak.

61219.q: What does Norway invest a large part of its North Sea oil income in?
a: A state fund for future generations
61219.e: Norway invests its oil income in the Government Pension Fund, one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world. This is meant to preserve the wealth even after the oil runs out.
61219.m: Norway saves its oil money in a huge state fund.

61220.q: Where does the money in Norway's sovereign wealth fund mainly come from?
61220.e: The state's income from oil and gas production flows into the fund. That is why it is often called the “oil fund”.
61220.m: Norway's sovereign wealth fund is fed by oil and gas income.

61221.q: Which institution manages Norway's sovereign wealth fund on behalf of the Ministry of Finance?
61221.e: It is managed by Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), part of the Norwegian central bank. The owner is the state, through the Ministry of Finance.
61221.m: The Norwegian central bank manages the sovereign wealth fund.

61222.q: Under the fiscal rule in force since 2017, what percentage of the fund's value may Norway use in the state budget each year?
61222.e: The fiscal rule allows roughly the expected real return to be spent each year, about 3 per cent since 2017. This preserves the capital for future generations.
61222.m: Norway spends only about 3 per cent of its oil fund each year.

61223.q: Why does Norway save its oil income in a fund instead of spending it straight away?
a: So that future generations also benefit from the oil
Because the constitution forbids state spending
Because the EU requires Norway to
So that the oil stays in the ground
61223.e: Oil and gas will run out one day. The fund invests the money, and the state uses only a small part of it each year. This preserves the wealth for later generations.
61223.m: The oil fund spreads Norway's oil wealth over many generations.

61224.q: Where does the Government Pension Fund Global invest its money?
61224.e: The fund invests its money only abroad, in shares, bonds, property and renewable energy infrastructure. This is to stop the domestic economy from overheating.
61224.m: The oil fund deliberately invests only outside Norway.

61225.q: Roughly what share of the value of all the world's listed companies does Norway's sovereign wealth fund hold (as of 2025)?
61225.e: The fund has stakes in about 8,500 companies and owns about 1.5 per cent of all listed shares worldwide (as of 2025). This makes it one of the largest investors in the world.
61225.m: The oil fund owns about one and a half per cent of all the world's shares.

61226.q: Which body has checked since 2004 whether companies should be excluded from Norway's sovereign wealth fund for ethical reasons?
61226.e: The Council on Ethics (Etikkrådet) was set up in 2004. It recommends, for example, excluding makers of certain weapons or companies that cause serious environmental damage.
61226.m: A Council on Ethics helps decide which companies the oil fund should avoid.

61227.q: Measured by its assets, what is Norway's sovereign wealth fund?
a: One of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world
A small fund only for fishermen's pensions
The largest fund in Scandinavia, but unimportant worldwide
A fund that only stores gold
61227.e: The fund was set up in 1990 and has grown through oil and gas income to well over 20,000 billion kroner. It is one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world.
61227.m: Norway's oil fund is one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world.

61228.q: Roughly what was the value of Norway's sovereign wealth fund in 2026?
61228.e: In mid-2026 its value was well over 20,000 billion Norwegian kroner, equivalent to about 2.3 trillion US dollars. It is one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world.
61228.m: The oil fund is worth over 20,000 billion kroner (as of 2026).

61229.q: Roughly what share of Norway's sovereign wealth fund was invested in shares in 2026?
61229.e: The largest part of the fund, about 70 per cent, is in shares. The rest is invested mainly in bonds and in property and renewable energy infrastructure.
61229.m: The oil fund invests most of its money in shares.

61230.q: In which German state do the Nord Stream pipelines come ashore?
61230.e: Both pipeline systems end at Lubmin near Greifswald in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. From there the gas was passed on into the European network.
61230.m: The Nord Stream pipelines come ashore in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

61231.q: In which Swiss canton did the operating company Nord Stream AG have its headquarters?
61231.e: Both Nord Stream AG and Nord Stream 2 AG were based in Zug. The majority owner was the Russian company Gazprom.
61231.m: The operators of the Nord Stream pipelines were based in Zug.

61232.q: What happened to the Nord Stream pipelines in September 2022?
a: They were badly damaged by explosions
61232.e: On 26 September 2022, explosions in the Baltic Sea near Bornholm ripped open three of the four pipeline strings. The investigation into who did it went on for a long time.
61232.m: In 2022 the Nord Stream pipelines were damaged by explosions.

61233.q: When did the first string of Nord Stream 1 go into operation?
61233.e: The first string started operating in November 2011, the second in October 2012. This meant Russian gas flowed directly to Germany without transit countries.

61234.q: From the operators' point of view, what was the main purpose of the Nord Stream pipelines?
61234.e: The pipelines ran through the Baltic Sea directly from Russia to Germany. This bypassed transit countries such as Ukraine, Poland and Belarus, which was controversial there.
61234.m: Nord Stream bypassed the transit countries via the Baltic Sea.

61235.q: When were three of the four strings of Nord Stream 1 and 2 damaged by explosions?
61235.e: On 26 September 2022, leaks caused by explosions were found near Bornholm. Both strings of Nord Stream 1 and one of Nord Stream 2 were destroyed.
61235.m: In September 2022 explosions destroyed most of the Nord Stream pipelines.

61236.q: Near which Danish island did the explosions on the Nord Stream pipelines happen?
61236.e: The leaks were in the Baltic Sea south-east and north-east of Bornholm, partly in Danish and partly in Swedish economic zones.
61236.m: The Nord Stream explosions happened near Bornholm.

61237.q: What happened to the approval process for Nord Stream 2 in February 2022?
a: Denmark refused permission to build it
61237.e: On 22 February 2022 Chancellor Olaf Scholz stopped the certification process in response to Russia's actions against Ukraine. The completed pipeline never went into operation.
61237.m: Nord Stream 2 was completed but never put into operation.

61238.q: Between which two countries did the Nord Stream pipelines run directly through the Baltic Sea?
61238.e: The pipelines ran from the Russian coast near Vyborg and Ust-Luga through the Baltic Sea to Lubmin in Germany. In this way, transit countries on land were bypassed.
61238.m: Nord Stream linked Russia and Germany directly through the Baltic Sea.

61239.q: Which two German states does the Lusatian lignite mining area lie in?
61239.e: The area lies in south-east Brandenburg and north-east Saxony. After the Rhineland area, it is the second largest lignite mining area in Germany.
61239.m: Lusatia is split between Brandenburg and Saxony.

61240.q: How is lignite mined in Lusatia?
a: In open-cast mines with huge excavators
61240.e: In Lusatia the lignite lies fairly close to the surface. Excavators first remove the layers of earth above it and then dig out the coal. Today the operator is the company LEAG.
61240.m: Lusatian lignite is extracted in open-cast mines.

61241.q: Which minority has been especially affected by resettlement for lignite mining in Lusatia?
61241.e: Lusatia is the homeland of the Slavic Sorbs (Wends). In the 20th century dozens of villages with a Sorbian character disappeared, for example Horno, which was resettled in the early 2000s.
61241.m: Many Sorbian villages had to make way for Lusatian coal.

61242.q: What is currently being created in many worked-out open-cast mines in Lusatia?
61242.e: Disused pits are flooded with water. This is creating the Lusatian Lake District, one of the largest artificial lake landscapes in Europe.
61242.m: Old open-cast mines are becoming the Lusatian Lake District.

61243.q: Why is the River Spree coloured brown in places downstream of the Lusatian open-cast mines?
a: Because of iron compounds from the mining areas
Because of coal dust from the power stations
Because of waste water from paper mills
Because of algal blooms in summer
61243.e: During mining, the mineral pyrite comes into contact with air and weathers. When the groundwater rises again, it washes iron and sulphate into the rivers, and iron ochre turns the water brown. This is called the “Brown Spree”.
61243.m: Iron ochre from old open-cast mines turns the Spree brown.

61244.q: What is the F60 in Lichterfeld, known as the “lying Eiffel Tower”?
a: A huge conveyor bridge from lignite mining
The cooling tower of a power station
61244.e: The F60 is over 500 metres long and is one of the largest movable machines in the world. In the open-cast mine it removed the layers of earth above the coal. Today it is a visitor attraction.
61244.m: The F60 is a huge conveyor bridge, the lying Eiffel Tower.

61245.q: Why is lignite more harmful to the climate per tonne and less productive than hard coal?
a: It contains more water and has a lower calorific value
It only burns with added gas
61245.e: Raw lignite often contains about 50 per cent water and has a low calorific value. More CO2 is therefore emitted for the same amount of electricity.
61245.m: Lignite is wet and has a low calorific value.

61246.q: Under the 2020 Coal Phase-Out Act, by when at the latest is Germany to stop generating electricity from coal?
61246.e: The 2020 Coal Phase-Out Act sets 2038 as the latest end date. For the Rhineland area, a phase-out by 2030 was later agreed.
61246.m: By 2038 at the latest, no more coal power is to be produced in Germany.

61247.q: Why do lignite power stations such as Jänschwalde usually stand right next to the open-cast mine?
a: Transporting the wet coal over long distances is not worth it
Coal transport is banned by law
They use mine water as fuel
61247.e: Raw lignite contains a lot of water and has a low calorific value. That is why it is usually taken by conveyor belt or works railway straight to the nearby power station and burned there.
61247.m: Lignite is turned into electricity close to the mine.

61248.q: How many nuclear reactors were in operation in France in 2024?
61248.e: With Flamanville 3 coming into service, 57 reactors were connected to the grid at the end of 2024. This makes France one of the countries with the most reactors in the world.

61249.q: Roughly what share of France's electricity comes from nuclear power (as of 2024)?
61249.e: Nuclear power supplies about two thirds of France's electricity, and in earlier years even over 70 per cent. No other large country has such a high share.
61249.m: In France about two thirds of electricity comes from nuclear power stations.

61250.q: Why did France decide in 1974 on a massive expansion of nuclear power?
a: To depend less on oil imports after the oil crisis
Because the EU required it of all members
Because hydropower was banned in France
Mainly to sell electricity to America
61250.e: The 1973 oil crisis showed how dependent France was on imported oil. Under the Messmer Plan, dozens of reactors were built over the next 15 years.
61250.m: The oil crisis made France a nuclear power nation.

61251.q: Which state-owned company operates all French nuclear power stations?
61251.e: Électricité de France (EDF) operates all the country's reactors. In 2023 EDF was fully nationalised again.
61251.m: EDF operates the French nuclear power stations.

61252.q: Which nuclear power station on the Rhine near the Swiss border was closed down in 2020?
61252.e: Fessenheim in Alsace was France's oldest nuclear power station and lay about 40 kilometres from Basel. Its two reactors were shut down in 2020.
61252.m: Fessenheim nuclear power station near Basel has been shut down since 2020.

61253.q: Which new type of reactor was built at Flamanville and started up there for the first time in 2024?
61253.e: Flamanville 3 is a European Pressurised Reactor (EPR). Construction began in 2007 and took about 17 years, and the costs rose enormously.
61253.m: Flamanville 3 is France's first EPR reactor.

61254.q: What happens at the La Hague plant in Normandy?
a: Final storage of highly radioactive waste
61254.e: At La Hague, spent fuel elements are taken apart chemically so that uranium and plutonium can be reused. Foreign customers, including Switzerland in the past, also had fuel reprocessed there.
61254.m: Spent fuel elements are reprocessed at La Hague.

61255.q: Why were a large number of French reactors shut down at the same time in 2022?
a: Because of corrosion and maintenance work
Because of a nuclear phase-out law
Because of a shortage of uranium from Russia
61255.e: At times more than half of the 56 reactors were offline, partly because of stress corrosion cracking in pipes. As a result, France had to import more electricity than it exported for the first time in decades.
61255.m: In 2022 corrosion damage put many French reactors out of action.

61256.q: Which plans for nuclear energy did President Macron announce in 2022?
a: Selling all power stations to private owners
61256.e: In Belfort in 2022, Macron announced the building of six new reactors of the EPR2 type, with an option for eight more. The first sites are Penly, Gravelines and Bugey.
61256.m: France is planning new EPR2 reactors instead of a nuclear phase-out.

61257.q: When was Germany's last nuclear power station taken off the grid?
61257.e: On 15 April 2023 Isar 2, Emsland and Neckarwestheim 2 were shut down. This completed Germany's nuclear phase-out.
61257.m: Since April 2023 Germany has produced no nuclear power.

61258.q: Which event in 2011 led to Germany's accelerated nuclear phase-out?
a: A fire at the Krümmel nuclear power station
61258.e: After the Fukushima nuclear disaster in March 2011, the Merkel government reversed the extension of reactor lifetimes it had agreed earlier. Eight reactors went offline immediately.
61258.m: Fukushima triggered Germany's fast nuclear phase-out in 2011.

61259.q: Which law of 2000 promoted renewable energy with fixed feed-in tariffs?
61259.e: The Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG) guaranteed operators of wind and solar plants fixed payments for 20 years. It became a model for many countries.
61259.m: The EEG of 2000 is the engine of Germany's energy transition.

61260.q: What did the term “Energiewende” (energy transition) mean when it was coined in 1980?
a: More nuclear power instead of coal
61260.e: The study “Energie-Wende. Growth and prosperity without oil and uranium” by the Öko-Institut appeared in 1980. The term was later adopted internationally.
61260.m: The term Energiewende comes from a study published in 1980.

61261.q: Roughly what share of Germany's electricity consumption was covered by renewable energy in 2023?
61261.e: In 2023 renewables covered over 50 per cent of gross electricity consumption for the first time. The most important source was wind energy.
61261.m: Since 2023 over half of Germany's electricity has come from renewable sources.

61262.q: According to its Climate Protection Act, by when does Germany want to be climate neutral?
61262.e: The Climate Protection Act, tightened in 2021, requires greenhouse gas neutrality by 2045. This puts Germany five years ahead of the EU target of 2050.
61262.m: Germany wants to be climate neutral by 2045.

61263.q: Why does the energy transition need new extra-high-voltage lines such as SuedLink?
a: Wind power from the north has to get to the south
Nuclear power from France has to get to the north
Coal power has to be exported to Poland
Solar power from the south has to get to the North Sea
61263.e: A lot of wind power is generated in northern Germany and at sea, while big consumers are in the south. SuedLink is meant to carry the electricity as direct current over hundreds of kilometres.
61263.m: SuedLink carries wind power from the north to the south of Germany.

61264.q: What happened to the EEG surcharge on German electricity bills in 2022?
a: It was renamed a coal levy
61264.e: Since July 2022 households no longer pay the EEG surcharge. Support for renewables has since been funded from the federal budget.
61264.m: The EEG surcharge was abolished in 2022.

61265.q: Which energy source in Germany was one of the first to benefit, from 1991, from the obligation to accept and pay for green electricity?
61265.e: The Electricity Feed-in Act of 1991 obliged electricity suppliers to accept electricity from renewable sources. It mainly helped early wind turbines and was a forerunner of the EEG.
61265.m: The Electricity Feed-in Act of 1991 was the forerunner of the EEG.

61266.q: Roughly what share of Denmark's electricity consumption was covered by wind energy in 2023?
61266.e: In 2023 Denmark covered more than half of its electricity needs with wind energy. That is one of the highest shares in the world.
61266.m: Denmark generates over half of its electricity from wind.

61267.q: In which decade did the world's first offshore wind farm go into operation off Denmark?
61267.e: The Vindeby wind farm off the island of Lolland went into operation in 1991 with eleven turbines. It ran for 25 years and was dismantled in 2017.
61267.m: In 1991 Denmark built the world's first offshore wind farm.

61268.q: Which Danish company, formerly DONG Energy, is one of the largest operators of offshore wind farms in the world?
61268.e: DONG Energy sold its oil and gas business and renamed itself Ørsted in 2017. The name honours the physicist Hans Christian Ørsted.
61268.m: DONG Energy became the wind company Ørsted.

61269.q: Which Danish manufacturer is one of the largest producers of wind turbines in the world?
61269.e: Vestas has its headquarters in Aarhus and has installed over 100 gigawatts of capacity worldwide. Siemens Gamesa is German-Spanish, while Enercon and Nordex are German.
61269.m: Vestas is a major Danish wind turbine maker.

61270.q: What did the Danish pioneer Poul la Cour research in Askov from 1891?
a: Oil production in the North Sea
61270.e: In Askov, Poul la Cour used wind power to generate electricity and stored the energy as hydrogen. He is considered the father of Danish wind energy.
61270.m: Poul la Cour is considered a pioneer of wind power generation.

61271.q: Which design is known as the “Danish concept” for wind turbines?
a: Three rotor blades on the windward side
Two blades on the leeward side
61271.e: Johannes Juul's Gedser turbine of 1957 set the standard: three blades turning in front of the tower, facing the wind. Almost all large turbines today follow this principle.
61271.m: Modern wind turbines follow the Danish concept with three blades.

61272.q: Why does Denmark build large wind farms such as Horns Rev at sea instead of on land?
a: At sea the wind blows more strongly and steadily
Building at sea is much cheaper
There are no storms at sea
The salt water generates extra electricity
61272.e: Over the sea, no hills, forests or houses slow the wind down. Offshore turbines therefore produce more electricity, even though building and maintenance cost more. Horns Rev 1, west of Esbjerg, went into operation in 2002 as the first large offshore wind farm.
61272.m: At sea the wind blows more strongly and steadily.

61273.q: Which major project is Denmark planning to bundle offshore wind power and send it to neighbouring countries?
a: Energy islands in the North Sea and the Baltic
A nuclear power station on Bornholm
61273.e: Denmark is planning energy islands, among other places near Bornholm, that will collect electricity from many wind farms. From there it is to be sent to Germany, for example.
61273.m: Danish energy islands are meant to collect and distribute wind power.

61274.q: How has Denmark particularly strengthened public acceptance of wind power?
a: Citizens can become co-owners of wind farms
Wind turbines stand only in uninhabited areas
Wind turbines are switched off at night
61274.e: At the Middelgrunden wind farm off Copenhagen, half of the 20 turbines belong to a cooperative with thousands of members. Such citizen participation has strengthened acceptance of wind power in Denmark.
61274.m: In Denmark many citizens have a stake in wind farms.

61275.q: Which technology does the Gemasolar solar power station near Seville use?
a: Solar tower with molten salt storage
61275.e: Thousands of mirrors focus sunlight onto a tower in which molten salt is heated. The heat store allows electricity to be produced at night as well.
61275.m: Thanks to its salt store, Gemasolar can also supply electricity at night.

61276.q: Which power station near Seville was Europe's first commercial solar tower power station in 2007?
61276.e: PS10 near Sanlúcar la Mayor was connected to the grid in 2007 and uses 624 mirrors that direct the light onto a tower. Gemasolar followed in 2011.
61276.m: PS10 near Seville was Europe's first commercial solar tower power station.

61277.q: What is the Plataforma Solar de Almería?
a: A large research centre for concentrated solar technology
The largest solar park in Europe
A port for importing solar cells
A factory for solar roof tiles
61277.e: The Plataforma Solar de Almería in Andalusia is Europe's largest research centre for solar thermal energy. Mirror power stations and storage systems are tested there.
61277.m: Concentrated solar technology is researched in Almería.

61278.q: Which technology do the Andasol power stations in the province of Granada use?
61278.e: Andasol uses long parabolic trough mirrors that heat a thermal oil. A salt store allows several hours of operation without sunshine.
61278.m: Andasol works with parabolic troughs and a salt store.

61279.q: Why is southern Spain especially well suited to solar energy?
a: Strong sunshine and many hours of sun
Lots of snow to reflect light
61279.e: With about 3,000 hours of sunshine a year, Andalusia and Extremadura are among the sunniest regions in Europe. There are also large, thinly populated areas.
61279.m: Southern Spain offers lots of sun and lots of space for solar plants.

61280.q: Which controversial charge on self-consumed solar power did Spain abolish in 2018?
a: The grid fee for wind farms
61280.e: A decree of 2015 placed charges on solar power used by the producers themselves, which was criticised as an “impuesto al sol” (sun tax). It was repealed in 2018, after which solar expansion picked up sharply.
61280.m: After the sun tax ended in 2018, solar energy boomed in Spain.

61281.q: In which Spanish region are large photovoltaic parks such as Núñez de Balboa and Francisco Pizarro?
61281.e: Both parks are in Extremadura, which borders Portugal, and with hundreds of megawatts they are among the largest solar parks in Europe.
61281.m: Extremadura is a stronghold of Spanish solar parks.

61282.q: What happened on the Iberian Peninsula on 28 April 2025 that fuelled the debate about grid stability with lots of solar power?
a: A record hailstorm on solar parks
The shutdown of all nuclear power stations
61282.e: On 28 April 2025 the power went off almost everywhere in Spain and Portugal for hours. Afterwards there was intense debate about how grids with a high share of solar power can stay stable.
61282.m: The 2025 blackout showed how important stable grids are.

61283.q: Roughly what share of Norway's electricity comes from hydropower?
61283.e: Norway generates about 90 per cent of its electricity from hydropower, making it the largest hydropower producer in Europe. By comparison, in Switzerland it is about 60 per cent.
61283.m: Norway gets almost all its electricity from hydropower.

61284.q: Which state-owned company is Norway's largest hydropower producer?
61284.e: Statkraft is wholly owned by the state and is considered the largest producer of renewable energy in Europe. It runs hundreds of hydropower stations.
61284.m: Statkraft is Norway's state hydropower company.

61285.q: Which undersea cable has connected Norway directly with Germany since 2021?
61285.e: NordLink is a direct current cable about 620 kilometres long between southern Norway and Schleswig-Holstein. It exchanges Norwegian hydropower for German wind power.
61285.m: NordLink connects Norwegian hydropower with Germany.

61286.q: Why is Norway often called the “battery of Europe”?
a: Its reservoirs can store energy and release it flexibly
It produces the most lithium batteries
It stores Europe's natural gas reserves
It has the largest coal stocks
61286.e: The large reservoirs hold about half of Europe's storage capacity. Water can be held back when wind and sun are producing a lot, and used to generate electricity when needed.
61286.m: Norway's reservoirs work like a giant battery.

61287.q: Which company was founded in 1905 to use hydropower to make artificial fertiliser?
61287.e: Norsk Hydro used the waterfalls near Rjukan and Notodden to make nitrogen fertiliser. Hydropower made Norway an industrial location early on.
61287.m: Norsk Hydro began in 1905 using hydropower for fertiliser.

61288.q: Why is Norway so well suited to hydropower?
a: Lots of rain and snow and big height differences down to the sea
Lakes that are frozen all year
61288.e: A lot of rain and snow falls on the mountains from the Atlantic. The water rushes down over big height differences to the coast, and hundreds of power stations use this energy.
61288.m: Rain and mountains make Norway a hydropower country.

61289.q: Which undersea cable has connected Norway with Great Britain since 2021 and was the longest undersea power cable in the world when it opened?
61289.e: North Sea Link runs about 720 kilometres from Kvilldal to Blyth in England. It allows electricity to be exchanged in both directions.
61289.m: North Sea Link connects Norway and Great Britain.

61290.q: What effect do dry years with little rain have on Norway's electricity market?
61290.e: When the reservoirs are low, there is not enough water to generate electricity. Prices then rise, as in southern Norway in 2022, and the country imports more electricity.
61290.m: In Norway, electricity prices depend heavily on the rain.

61291.q: Which undersea cable, opened in 2008, connects Norway with the Netherlands?
61291.e: NorNed is about 580 kilometres long and was the longest undersea power cable in the world when it opened. It allows electricity trading between the two countries.
61291.m: Since 2008 NorNed has connected Norway with the Netherlands.

61292.q: When did the Chernobyl nuclear disaster happen?
61292.e: In the night of 26 April 1986, Unit 4 of the Chernobyl nuclear power station exploded. It was the worst accident in the history of civil nuclear power.

61293.q: What did the Chernobyl reactor lack compared with most Western nuclear power stations?
a: A strong protective shell of steel and concrete
A connection to the power grid
61293.e: The Soviet RBMK reactor type had no full containment. That is why, after the explosion, large amounts of radioactive material escaped into the air unhindered.
61293.m: Chernobyl lacked a strong protective shell around the reactor.

61294.q: What was being carried out in Reactor 4 at Chernobyl on the night of the accident?
61294.e: The aim was to test whether the turbines, as they ran down, would supply enough power for the cooling pumps. Operating errors and design faults led to the explosion.
61294.m: A failed safety test triggered the disaster.

61295.q: Which town near the power station was completely evacuated a day after the accident?
61295.e: Pripyat, the town of the power station workers with about 49,000 inhabitants, was evacuated on 27 April 1986. It is still a ghost town today.
61295.m: After Chernobyl, Pripyat became a ghost town.

61296.q: In which country was the increased radioactivity after Chernobyl first noticed in the West?
61296.e: On 28 April 1986, measuring instruments at the Swedish nuclear power station of Forsmark raised the alarm. This is how the world learned of the accident, which the Soviet Union at first kept quiet.
61296.m: Sweden was the first Western country to detect the radiation from Chernobyl.

61297.q: Which part of Switzerland was most affected by radioactive fallout from Chernobyl?
61297.e: Heavy rain in early May 1986 washed radioactive particles out of the air over Ticino. Fishing bans were imposed there, for example on Lake Lugano.
61297.m: Ticino received the most Chernobyl fallout in Switzerland.

61298.q: What is the protective shell called that was slid over the damaged reactor in 2016?
61298.e: The huge arch structure was built next to the reactor and slid over it in November 2016. It replaces the crumbling sarcophagus of 1986 and is meant to last about 100 years.
61298.m: Since 2016 the New Safe Confinement has covered the damaged reactor.

61299.q: What is the half-life of caesium-137, which made up a large part of the long-term contamination after Chernobyl?
61299.e: Caesium-137 decays with a half-life of about 30 years. That is why wild boar and mushrooms in some areas are still contaminated today. About 8 days is the half-life of iodine-131.
61299.m: Caesium-137 has a half-life of about 30 years.

61300.q: What was the radius of the original exclusion zone around the Chernobyl nuclear power station?
61300.e: After the accident, an exclusion zone with a radius of about 30 kilometres was set up. Over 100,000 people had to leave their homes.
61300.m: There is an exclusion zone of about 30 kilometres around Chernobyl.

61301.q: At which level of the International Nuclear Event Scale (INES) is Chernobyl rated?
61301.e: Chernobyl received the highest INES level, 7, a “major accident”. Only Fukushima in 2011 was rated the same.
61301.m: With INES level 7, Chernobyl counts as a major accident.

61302.q: In which country is the iron ore town of Kiruna?
61302.e: Kiruna lies in Lapland in the far north of Sweden, north of the Arctic Circle. It is the country's northernmost town.
61302.m: Kiruna is in northern Sweden, north of the Arctic Circle.

61303.q: Who owns LKAB, the company that runs the huge iron ore mine in Kiruna?
61303.e: Luossavaara-Kiirunavaara Aktiebolag (LKAB) is wholly owned by the Swedish state. The mine in the Kiirunavaara mountain is the largest underground iron ore mine in the world.
61303.m: Through LKAB, the Kiruna mine belongs to the Swedish state.

61304.q: Through which ice-free port is a large part of Kiruna's ore exported?
61304.e: Since 1902 the Ore Railway has linked Kiruna with Narvik in Norway. Thanks to the Gulf Stream, the port is ice-free all year, while Luleå freezes in winter.
61304.m: Kiruna ore goes out to the world through ice-free Narvik.

61305.q: Why is Kiruna's town centre being moved to a new location?
a: Mining is causing the ground to sink
A glacier is threatening the town
The permafrost is thawing too much
A dam is to be built
61305.e: Mining under the town causes ground movements and cracks. That is why the centre is being moved about 3 kilometres to the east; the new centre opened in 2022.
61305.m: Kiruna is moving because mining is making the ground sink.

61306.q: What is the ore from Kiruna mainly used for?
61306.e: Kiruna mainly mines magnetite, an iron oxide. It is processed into pellets and delivered to steelworks.
61306.m: Iron ore from Kiruna is made into steel.

61307.q: What did LKAB announce for the Kiruna region in January 2023?
a: The largest known deposit of rare earths in Europe
The closure of the mine by 2025
The building of a nuclear power station
61307.e: LKAB reported the largest known deposit of rare earth elements in Europe. These metals are needed, for example, for electric motors and wind turbines.
61307.m: Europe's largest known deposit of rare earths lies near Kiruna.

61308.q: Why is mining in Kiruna no longer done in an open pit but underground?
a: The ore body reaches steeply down to great depths
Open-pit mining is banned in the polar winter
The ore at the surface was radioactive
The open pit lay under a lake
61308.e: Mining began in an open pit in 1898. Because the ore body runs steeply downwards, an open pit would have become wider and more expensive all the time. Today the main level is about 1,365 metres deep.
61308.m: In Kiruna, mining follows the ore far down into the depths.

61309.q: Why was iron ore from Kiruna strategically important in the Second World War?
a: It was an important raw material for German arms production
It was needed for atomic bombs
It was used as fuel for ships
It was Europe's only source of gold
61309.e: Germany got a large part of its iron ore from northern Sweden, partly through Narvik. The battle for Narvik in 1940 was also linked to these ore supplies.
61309.m: Kiruna ore was important for Germany's arms production in the Second World War.

61310.q: Which Swedish project aims to use ore from Kiruna to make steel with hydrogen instead of coal?
61310.e: HYBRIT is a project of SSAB, LKAB and Vattenfall. Instead of coke, hydrogen is used to reduce the iron ore, which produces almost no CO2.
61310.m: HYBRIT aims to make fossil-free steel with hydrogen.

61311.q: What is the decentralised data exchange platform called through which authorities and companies in Estonia have exchanged data securely since 2001?
61311.e: X-Road (X-tee in Estonian) connects the databases of authorities and companies without storing all the data centrally. It is considered the technical backbone of Estonian e-government.
61311.m: In Estonia, X-Road connects the state's databases.

61312.q: Which service did Estonia introduce at the end of 2014 that allows foreigners to get a digital identity from the country?
61312.e: With e-Residency, people from all over the world receive an Estonian digital identity, for example to set up and run a company in the EU online. It is neither citizenship nor a right of residence.
61312.m: E-Residency gives foreigners an Estonian digital identity.

61313.q: What has Estonia been known for worldwide since the local elections of 2005?
a: Legally binding voting over the internet
61313.e: In 2005 Estonia was the first country to hold legally binding internet elections nationwide; since 2007 this has also applied to parliamentary elections. Voters identify themselves with the electronic ID card.
61313.m: Since 2005 Estonia has allowed voting over the internet nationwide.

61314.q: Which well-known internet telephone service was developed largely by Estonian programmers in 2003?
61314.e: Skype's software was programmed by the Estonians Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn. Its success is seen as the starting signal for the Estonian start-up scene.
61314.m: Skype was developed by Estonian programmers.

61315.q: Which event in 2007 brought down the websites of Estonian banks, media and authorities?
a: A fire in the central data centre
61315.e: After the dispute over moving the Soviet Bronze Soldier in Tallinn, Estonia was hit by massive overload attacks (DDoS) in April and May 2007. The case is considered one of the first cyber attacks on an entire state.
61315.m: In 2007 Estonia was the target of massive cyber attacks.

61316.q: Which NATO institution was founded in Tallinn in 2008?
a: A centre of excellence for cyber defence
61316.e: The Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE) in Tallinn researches questions of cyber security and international law in cyberspace. It was set up partly in response to Estonia's experience of cyber attacks.
61316.m: NATO's cyber defence centre is in Tallinn.

61317.q: What was the aim of the Estonian schools programme “Tiger Leap” from 1996?
a: To equip all schools with computers and the internet
61317.e: From 1996 the Tiigrihüpe (“Tiger Leap”) programme brought computers and the internet to all Estonian schools. It is seen as an early basis for the population's high digital skills.
61317.m: In the 1990s, Tiger Leap brought the internet to Estonia's schools.

61318.q: What is the Estonian “data embassy” in Luxembourg?
a: A protected server site with backup copies of state data
An embassy that can only be contacted by email
An archive for old paper files
61318.e: In 2017 Estonia and Luxembourg agreed on the world's first data embassy, a server site with diplomatic protection. This keeps important state data available even if Estonia itself is attacked.
61318.m: Estonia's data embassy is in Luxembourg.

61319.q: What does the “once-only principle” used in Estonia mean?
a: The state may only ask citizens for data once
Everyone may only vote online once
Every authority has only one website
Passwords may only be used once
61319.e: Under the once-only principle, a person only has to give the state the same information once. Other authorities then get it themselves through the secure data exchange.
61319.m: Under the once-only principle, you only have to give the state the same data once.

61320.q: Which landscape in the Gauja valley around Sigulda is also called “Livonian Switzerland” because of its hills and sandstone cliffs?
61320.e: Gauja National Park, founded in 1973, is Latvia's oldest national park. The deeply cut river valley with castles and caves reminded travellers of Switzerland.
61320.m: The area around Sigulda is also called Livonian Switzerland.

61321.q: Which medieval league of towns did Riga belong to as an important trading city?
61321.e: Riga was founded in 1201 and later joined the Hanseatic League. Via the River Daugava, the city traded in timber, furs and grain from the hinterland.

61322.q: For which architecture is the centre of Riga especially famous?
61322.e: Riga has one of the largest collections of Art Nouveau buildings in the world; a large part of the buildings in the centre date from around 1900. Many were designed by the architect Mikhail Eisenstein.
61322.m: Riga is famous for its many Art Nouveau buildings.

61323.q: Which spa town with a sandy beach over 30 kilometres long lies west of Riga on the Gulf of Riga?
61323.e: Jūrmala is made up of a row of former fishing villages and seaside resorts on a narrow strip of land. It is known for its wooden villas and spas.
61323.m: Jūrmala is Latvia's best-known seaside resort.

61324.q: In which year did Latvia introduce the euro?
61324.e: Latvia replaced the lats with the euro on 1 January 2014. The country had already joined the EU in 2004.
61324.m: Latvia has paid with the euro since 2014.

61325.q: What is the historic region in the west of Latvia on the Baltic coast called?
61325.e: Courland (Kurzeme in Latvian) covers western Latvia, with ports such as Liepāja and Ventspils. Latgale lies in the east, Livonia in the north-east and Semigallia in the south.
61325.m: Courland is Latvia's western coastal region.

61326.q: With which of these countries does Latvia not share a land border?
61326.e: Latvia borders Estonia, Russia, Belarus and Lithuania. Poland is separated from Latvia by Lithuania.

61327.q: What was the human chain called that stretched from Tallinn via Riga to Vilnius on 23 August 1989?
61327.e: About two million people formed a chain over 600 kilometres long to remember the Hitler-Stalin Pact of 1939 and to demand independence. The Baltic Way is part of UNESCO's Memory of the World register.
61327.m: In 1989 the Baltic Way linked the three Baltic capitals.

61328.q: Which tradition of the Baltic states is part of UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage and plays a big role in Latvia?
a: The great song and dance festivals
61328.e: The song and dance festivals with tens of thousands of participants take place in Latvia about every five years. They also strengthened national identity during the Soviet era.
61328.m: The song and dance festivals are a shared cultural heritage of the Baltic states.

61329.q: Which island castle from the 14th and 15th centuries stands on an island in Lake Galvė west of Vilnius?
61329.e: Trakai Island Castle was a residence of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania. It was rebuilt from ruins in the 20th century.
61329.m: Trakai Island Castle was the seat of the Lithuanian Grand Dukes.

61330.q: Why was Kaunas the temporary capital of Lithuania between the two World Wars?
a: Because Vilnius had been destroyed in the war
Because Kaunas is by the sea
Because the king lived in Kaunas
61330.e: Poland occupied Vilnius in 1920 and kept the city until 1939. During this time hundreds of modern buildings were built in Kaunas, which have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023.
61330.m: Kaunas was the capital while Vilnius belonged to Poland.

61331.q: In which year did Lithuania declare its independence as the first Soviet republic to do so?
61331.e: On 11 March 1990 the Supreme Soviet of Lithuania declared the restoration of independence. The Soviet Union only recognised it in September 1991.
61331.m: In 1990 Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence.

61332.q: What is the Hill of Crosses in Lithuania known for?
a: Tens of thousands of crosses as a sign of resistance
A monastery with the largest bell in Europe
A First World War military cemetery
61332.e: On the hill near Šiauliai, pilgrims have put up tens of thousands of crosses over the decades. The Soviet authorities had it flattened several times, but people kept putting up new crosses.
61332.m: The Hill of Crosses near Šiauliai is a symbol of Lithuanian resistance.

61333.q: Which union joined Lithuania and Poland into a single state from 1569?
61333.e: The Union of Lublin in 1569 created the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth with a shared king and parliament. It lasted until the partitions of Poland at the end of the 18th century.
61333.m: In 1569 the Union of Lublin created the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

61334.q: Which special feature do linguists attribute to the Lithuanian language?
a: It is considered a particularly archaic Indo-European language
It is closely related to Hungarian
It is written in Cyrillic letters
61334.e: Lithuanian has kept many old forms, for example a rich system of cases, and is therefore important for research into the Indo-European parent language. It is written in the Latin alphabet.
61334.m: Lithuanian is considered one of the most archaic living Indo-European languages.

61335.q: According to calculations by the French National Geographic Institute in 1989, where is the geographical centre of Europe?
